blocks.text: From October 22 to December 19, 2026, Villazan hosts Makos. Inside , the first solo exhibition in Spain of the American photographer Christopher Makos . Pilar Giró is the curator and has chosen sixteen images for the occasion, from Andy Warhol to Jean-Michel Basquiat, David Hockney to Salvador Dalí, Mick Jagger to Pedro Almodóvar and Alaska.
A native of Massachusetts, Makos moved to New York around 1970 after years in California..
Warhol in focus

Andy Warhol, whom Makos came to know in the 1970s, has a large share of the selection. It includes images from Altered Image ( Lady Warhol ), a series made in 1981 in which the artist plays along with rouge and wigs.
The Spanish angle
Three names tie the show most directly to the Madrid public: Alaska, Pedro Almodóvar, and Salvador Dalí, all photographed by Makos.
The Madrid presentation is the first opportunity to see his work in a dedicated space in Spain.
Curatorial text by Pilar Giró

Christopher Makos belongs to a generation of photographers for whom the camera, beyond being a tool of observation, was also a way of being in the world. Born in Massachusetts, he built his life between California and New York, and found in photography a language for approaching people, places, and the culture of his time. His arrival in New York in the early 1970s coincided with one of the city’s moments of greatest creative effervescence, when art, music, film, fashion, and nightlife shared spaces, languages, and protagonists. Makos did not contemplate that world from the outside: he was part of it.

The selection of photographs gathered in the exhibition MAKOS. INSIDE distills, without claiming to exhaust it, his dimension as a photographer: his closeness to his subjects, his curiosity, and above all his ability to capture what defines a person and the cultural time surrounding them. Makos has explained that he needs to know the person he photographs, to talk with them, to establish a relationship before pressing the shutter. Hence the naturalness running through so many of his portraits, and the sense of standing before images that, while belonging to a very specific moment, seem to escape it.

Sixteen photographs that move through different territories of his career and make it possible to understand just how far his photography was able to capture a culture in transformation. Among the images appear figures from art, music, fashion, and film: David Hockney, Keith Haring, Jean-Michel Basquiat, Mick Jagger, or Tom Ford, not as a succession of celebrities but as fragments of a single cultural constellation. The exhibition brings together precisely that transversality: disciplines we tend to separate today appear here connected by a shared energy and a shared way of understanding creation.

Andy Warhol inevitably holds a central place. Makos met him in the 1970s, and a relationship of friendship, complicity, and creative exchange developed between them, yielding some of the most recognizable images of his career. In the series Altered Image , also known as Lady Warhol , the portrait becomes a space for experimentation. Warhol appears in makeup and various wigs, deliberately shifting the codes of gender, identity, and representation. These photographs, made in 1981, do not simply document a physical transformation: they make identity something mutable, constructed, and open.

The exhibition also allows us to recognize Makos’s close relationship with the art world. Hockney, Haring, Basquiat, and Warhol appear before his camera without the solemnity that art history would come to bestow on them. Makos photographs them from a closeness that preserves something of the moment before they became icons. Perhaps that is one of the most singular qualities of his work: his photographs do not seem to pursue posterity, and yet they end up building it.

At VILLAZAN, the exhibition also takes on a particular resonance through the images linked to Spain. Salvador Dalí appears as part of that international universe in which the boundaries between art, entertainment, and public persona were blurring. Pedro Almodóvar and Alaska introduce another geography and another generation, but also a kindred sensibility: freedom as an attitude, experimentation with identity, and the will to transform established cultural codes. Their presence broadens the narrative and reminds us that Makos’s eye was never confined to a single scene.

More than documenting his subjects, Makos captured what was happening around them: the intensity of a cultural moment, the relationships between disciplines, the energy of a generation, and a certain idea of freedom. His images were born of the immediate, but have become part of our visual memory. We do not merely recognize those who appear in them; through these photographs, we recognize a way of imagining an entire era.

Perhaps that is why his work retains such a contemporary force today. Makos has the ability to fix the instant without locking it into its time. His vision transforms what is observed into image and the moment into memory; he turns the immediate into something that ends up seeming classic.
Pilar Giró
